rss_3_1785526785.title: The power of ignorance and peering into the Milky Way: Books in brief
rss_3_1785526785.text:
Smog and Sunshine Ann Carlson Univ. California Press (2026)

From the 1940s to the 1990s, smoggy Los Angeles, California, had “stunningly unhealthy air”, writes environmental lawyer Ann Carlson. Now, it is “remarkably clean”. Her powerful book details how scientists, lawyers and residents collaborated with public officials to reduce pollution, especially from vehicles, beginning with the state’s first Clean Air Act in 1963. Today, however, air pollution is growing again as a result of wildfires driven by climate change.

Ignorance George Szpiro Columbia Univ. Press (2026)

Unlike knowledge, ignorance receives little systematic study and is often regarded negatively, observes journalist George Szpiro. But ignorance has a “redeeming feature”, he argues: “it motivates curiosity and drives the quest for knowledge.” His penetrating book examines 60 well-known instances of ignorance divided into four categories: ‘do not know’ (for example, dark matter), ‘cannot know’ (the uncertainty principle), ‘must not know’ (the placebo effect) and ‘refuse to know’ (disaster insurance).

Radio Universe Emma Chapman John Murray (2026)

Radio telescopes can penetrate the Venusian atmosphere, reveal underground lakes beneath the Martian surface, and look through the “bright heart of the Milky Way to the spiral arms beyond”, observes astrophysicist Emma Chapman. Her captivating book introduces radioastronomy by glorying in such achievements. Part I focuses on the Solar System, part II on our Galaxy and part III on the Universe, including dark matter and dark energy. Chapman also discusses radioastronomy’s role in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence.

The Irrational Decision Benjamin Recht Princeton Univ. Press (2026)

rss_4_1785526786.title: Meat allergy is on the rise — what scientists want to know
rss_4_1785526786.text:
Bites from a lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum), which live on white-tailed deer, are the main cause of α-gal allergy in the United States.Credit: BackyardProduction/Getty

Thomas Platts-Mills develops a rash if he eats red meat. The immunologist is one of thousands of people who are diagnosed each year with tick-induced α-gal allergy — a life-threatening allergy that is on the rise.

People can develop the allergy after being bitten at least twice by ticks that carry a sugar molecule called α-gal (galactose α-1,3 galactose) in their saliva. Ticks are often carried on deer and can be transmitted to a human host when people walk through grasses or past shrubs that contain the parasites.

Cases of α-gal allergy are increasing in many countries. Researchers say climate change and rising deer populations are contributing factors, but there is much that scientists don’t understand about the disease. Even diagnosing it is difficult because people mostly experience vague symptoms, such as stomach pain or vomiting, hours after eating meat, and sometimes months after a tick bite. For this reason, the allergy is probably under-diagnosed. There is currently no treatment or cure.

“We’re still casting in the dark, but it is our responsibility to find something that works for people” in need of treatment, says Benjamin Casterline, an immunology researcher at the University of Missouri School of Medicine in Columbia.

When a tick bites, α-gal is transferred from the saliva into the person’s blood, triggering the production of immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibodies. Future exposures to α-gal, which is found in red meat and dairy products, can trigger an allergic reaction. For some people, this can be life-threatening anaphylaxis, says Platts-Mills, who also studies allergies at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville. At least two people have died worldwide because of the allergy.

On the rise

Australia has the highest rates of α-gal allergy in the world — affecting more than 700 people out of 100,000 in some tick-prone regions. Suspected cases have increased by 22% each year since 2020, with most caused by the Australian paralysis tick (Ixodes holocyclus).

The United States is also a hotspot, and as many as 450,000 people might have the allergy, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Between 2017 and 2022, around 15,000 people each year were newly diagnosed with the allergy, with most cases occurring in regions where the lone star tick (Amblyomma americanum) is common — bites from this tick species are the main cause of α-gal allergy in the United States.

In Japan, 2–4% of the population (up to 4.9 million people) have been exposed to α-gal and produced antibodies, meaning that they are sensitized to the molecule, but are not necessarily allergic to it. In Denmark, the prevalence of α-gal sensitization in the population more than doubled between 1990 and 2016 — from 1.3% to 3.2%. One study found that 1–8% of people living in areas with high tick populations have the allergy, and up to 35% of people might be sensitized1.

Climate change is one explanation for the increase in cases, as warming temperatures increase tick habitats, says Nanju Alice Lee, a food scientist and allergy researcher at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia. For example, Australian tick habitats were previously restricted to a small area of New South Wales but have expanded across the country’s east coast into Queensland, Lee says.

Growing deer populations are another reason for the rise in the United States, says Platt-Mills. White-tailed deer (Odocoileus virgianus) are the main host for the lone star tick and have been increasing beyond their usual habitat, as have roe deer (Capreolus capreolus) populations in Denmark, which are hosts for the castor bean tick (Ixodes ricinus), the main cause of α-gal allergy in Europe .

An unusual allergy

rss_6_1785526789.title: How smallpox reached the Americas: first genomic evidence points to Europeans
rss_6_1785526789.text:
Atahualpa, the last Incan emperor, was seized by troops in 1532 during the Spanish Conquest, but smallpox had already devastated the Inca Empire around 1524–1528.Credit: Florilegius/Alamy

More than 400 years ago, two people living in modern day Chile died while infected with the smallpox virus. Viral DNA found in their mummified remains has now yielded genetic evidence of when the disease arrived in the Americas.

The findings, published on 30 July in Science1, confirm that Orthopoxvirus variola — the virus that causes smallpox — arrived in the Americas from Europe. The study adds to a small but growing body of evidence that the smallpox virus lost genes as it adapted to human hosts, a mechanism that related viruses, such as the one that causes mpox, might also be using today.

“We don’t know anything about the recent history of viruses,” says Terry Jones, a computational virologist at Charité — University Medicine Berlin. Studies such as this provide a rare snapshot into a pathogen’s past, he says.

Surprise smallpox

Smallpox was one of the deadliest diseases in the world. The virus killed an estimated 300 million people in the twentieth century alone. Historical records suggest that its introduction into the Americas was similarly catastrophic, killing millions of people across two continents.

However, viruses don’t leave much archaeological evidence. So far, there are only two examples of smallpox DNA from before the twentieth century: a set of sequences from seventh-century Viking remains, and a single sequence from a seventeenth-century Lithuanian mummy.

What limited genetic evidence researchers do have suggests that smallpox has undergone intense evolution over the centuries. The seventh-century virus genome is much larger and contains more active genes than do twentieth-century smallpox strains.

Smallpox and other viruses plagued humans much earlier than suspected

This latest study found smallpox by accident. The team was originally testing DNA analysis software as a way to study the human history of an archaeological site in northern Chile. To do this, researchers had sequenced DNA from the remains of two people who lived in a small settlement some time between 1492 and 1631.

To their surprise, the analysis also uncovered traces of an unknown smallpox variant. Finding traces of the disease “didn’t cross my mind”, says co-author Constanza de la Fuente Castro, a biological anthropologist at the University of Chile in Santiago. But that “makes it even more exciting”.

The team then compared the variant to other ancient and modern smallpox genomes. What they found suggested that the Chilean variant split off from a European branch of the disease around the thirteenth century, confirming that European colonizers were the source of smallpox in the region.

rss_7_1785526791.title: Scientists using LLMs will ‘do more, less well’, modelling study predicts
rss_7_1785526791.text:
The rising use of artificial-intelligence tools by scientists could increase their productivity, but this might come at the cost of quality.Credit: Getty

Scientists who use large language models (LLMs) to help them with their research will spend less time refining their work and instead jump quickly to fresh projects, according to a modelling study1.

Adoption of LLMs will cause scientists to “do more, less well — rather than the same amount, better”, write the authors. But they say that such artificial-intelligence tools do not bear all of the blame for that outcome.

The results reflect a flawed incentive system in science that prioritizes quantity over quality, says study co-author Carl Bergstrom, a biologist at the University of Washington in Seattle. Scientists are incentivized to churn out papers, he says, and LLMs help them to reach this ever-growing quota. “LLMs are rarely the problem themselves,” says Bergstrom. “LLMs hold up a mirror to problems that we already have.” The study was posted on the arXiv preprint repository on 19 July and has not yet been peer reviewed.

Foraging for papers

To predict how LLMs will change scientific productivity, the authors broke the research process into discrete phases. First comes a discovery phase when scientists brainstorm hypotheses and conduct initial experiments to determine the value of a project. Next, there is a two-part development phase that consists of required work (such as creating figures and drafting papers) and discretionary development (such as conducting follow-up experiments and polishing writing).

The authors drew on methods from optimal-foraging theory — which analyses how an animal maximizes energy gain while conserving resources — to analyse how scientists will reallocate their efforts after incorporating LLMs into their work. The authors’ model assumed LLMs are functioning at their best — cheap, fast and accurate.

AI linked to explosion of low-quality biomedical research papers

The modelling predicts that LLMs can speed up all phases of the scientific process, but that this acceleration won’t result in better papers. Faster discovery and required-work phases mean that researchers can churn out papers more quickly than they could without the help of LLMs, and the pressure to publish means there is little incentive to spend extra time polishing those papers.

Quality not quantity

rss_8_1785526792.title: Somatic mutations reveal the ontogeny of microglia in human aging
rss_8_1785526792.text: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the central nervous system1. In mice, microglia seed the brain during embryogenesis and can be maintained throughout life with minimal input from adult hematopoiesis2-4. The origins of human microglia are less clear, but recent evidence suggests that marrow-derived cells contribute to the human microglial pool in certain individuals5-9. Here, to investigate the ontogeny of human microglia, we develop an approach that uses the collection of accumulated somatic mutations which uniquely labels each clone of cells to track the infiltration of marrow-derived cells into the human brain. Applying this approach to 20 aged individuals, we find evidence of an influx of marrow-derived cells into the brain in all examined individuals. Single cell analysis, including single cell lineage tracing using mitochondrial DNA variants, demonstrates that these infiltrating cells are similar to microglia and can comprise a large fraction of the microglial pool. Analysis of human cohort data demonstrates a protective association between most types of clonal hematopoiesis and Alzheimer’s disease. In sum, this work uncovers a widespread influx of myeloid cells into the healthy human brain which contributes to the pool of human microglia and becomes common with aging.

rss_10_1785526795.title: Job insecurity is chipping away at me and my cohort. Is it us, or the state of the economy?
rss_10_1785526795.text:
Job hunting in the current economic climate can feel like a futile task for many early-career researchers.Credit: Amit Basu/Getty

I am struggling to find job security. Over the past two years, I’ve been rejected for positions as a senior research fellow, a lecturer and a research funding manager. My initial one-year contract, which was extended to 2.5 years, officially ends in three months. Every application feels like a lottery ticket. Every rejection feels personal, even when I know it shouldn’t. It’s as if I’m no longer good enough to be in academia. The stress is building. I feel like my career is at stake and, even more urgently, I’m starting to ask myself difficult questions about how to pay my rent once my contract runs out.

I know I’m not alone. At least five friends and colleagues at a similar career stage are also applying for jobs with months, or even weeks, left on their current contracts. It’s difficult to aim for independence as a researcher by landing a fellowship or getting a permanent position while navigating a career stage filled with fixed-term contracts.

My relationship with my PhD supervisor has become toxic — what do I do?

I hold a PhD in behavioural science, as well as a doctorate-equivalent qualification required to become a chartered health psychologist. I currently work as a researcher on the mental-health impacts of climate change at Imperial College London, one of the world’s leading universities.

And I’ve done what you’re supposed to do to make it in academia: I’ve published papers, won research grants and consultancy funding, taught across disciplines and co-hosted a United Nations webinar on what solutions young people want to improve their mental well-being during the climate crisis. I’ve also presented and strategized at a European Commission meeting on climate and health, and have been featured on the BBC World Service’s The Climate Question.

I work with several youth-led organizations, co-lead the lived-experience advisory board for the Lancet Psychiatry Commission on climate change and mental health, and deliver training on how to have difficult conversations about the climate, including at the Natural History Museum in London. I have academic mentors supporting me. Outside academia, I have worked in several sectors, including for charities and non-governmental organizations aiding hurricane recovery in the Caribbean.

Many people have achieved much more, but on paper I hoped that I looked like someone who should feel secure in their academic career.

Identifying the issues

So, myself and my colleagues find ourselves whispering the same question: is this a personal failing, or a symptom of a wider systemic shift in academia? A meta-analysis published in Nature Human Behaviour in June1 reported that early-career researchers have a greater prevalence of symptoms of mental ill health, such as depression and anxiety, compared with the general population. Job insecurity is listed as one of the stressors. I feel especially drawn to this issue because, as a health psychologist, I can see how allowing this period of uncertainty to become a period of self-criticism could damage my health and be unhelpful in my job hunt.

Postdoc depression and anxiety rates are rising, finds survey of 872 researchers

Conferring with academic mentors, I can recognize why this is happening, and why it might not entirely be to do with my personal abilities and is instead about the wider world and many circumstances that are out of my control.

The job market does not exist in a vacuum. Global conflicts have driven energy prices up and destabilized economies. In the United States, the administration of President Donald Trump has shifted science funding priorities, causing ripples across global health and climate funding. In the United Kingdom, where I live, projections show fewer vacancies and rising unemployment — pressures that hit low- and middle-income countries particularly hard. These changes cascade through research ecosystems, reducing opportunities and intensifying competition. Professors are also feeling the pinch.

Another driver of competition is the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence to assist in the writing of grant and job applications. This has clear benefits for many individual researchers, who can now produce stronger applications, but it also means that competitive applicants can produce even more polished proposals. The net result is that the total number of submissions has surged. Review systems, already stretched, are buckling under the volume of applications. In response, the European Research Council introduced (and soon scrapped, after backlash) a major change that would have seen applicants whose funding applications did not score highly enough unable to reapply for up to four years.

In much of the world, it’s a hard time to be looking for work in any sector.

Competing in an impossible market

I first started to feel panic in July 2024, 18 months before my contract was due to end. I began applying for academic fellowships, widely seen as the next step at my career stage. As my contract’s end date approached this January, I won a small pot of funding to sustain me for an extra six months.

With the clock ticking on my contract, and limited success to show from my applications, I shifted from attempting to win research funding through fellowships to applying for a wider scope of academic and non-academic positions. But the time required to complete each type of application forces difficult choices. You cannot do everything while performing at a full-time job (see ‘Practical support for struggling jobseekers’).

Practical support for struggling jobseekers Many of us are navigating the same pressures, as well as the same quiet fear of not being enough. There is power in remembering that your worth is not determined by a reviewer’s score, a funding panel’s decision or a job market in crisis. As a health psychologist, I want to share coping strategies to use when job hunting, for those who are also struggling. Five practical ways to support yourself: 1. Reach out to peers in similar situations, because it can be validating and grounding. 2. Seek mentors who can offer strategic guidance and share stories about their rejections, to normalize them. 3. If your institution or colleagues offer support to prepare for applications and interviews, take up the offer. 4. Ask for feedback on applications or interviews — really reflect on this and use what you’ve learnt. 5. Give yourself time to process a rejection before throwing yourself back into work. Go for a walk or speak to someone supportive.

Developing a fellowship proposal takes around a year and repurposing it for a different funder takes another three months. Academic job applications require about three full days to properly tune a CV, read up on the group’s literature and develop your research plan for the next five years. Adjusting a CV and drafting a cover letter for non-academic roles, by contrast, takes me around three hours.

rss_11_1785526796.title: Demand for lithium is surging: here’s how to make mining more sustainable
rss_11_1785526796.text:
Lithium salts being recovered from brine pools in South America.Credit: Martin Bernetti/AFP via Getty

As more people seek out electric vehicles and batteries to store renewable energy, demand for lithium, the metal at the core of most rechargeable batteries, is intensifying. But mining lithium has substantial impacts on the environment. A wave of innovative technologies could make its extraction more sustainable.

Electric vehicles accounted for more than one-quarter of all global car sales last year, according to the International Energy Agency. The agency projects that demand for lithium for electric vehicles could reach around 665 kilotonnes by 2035. Yet, planned and existing mining projects would produce only about 450 kilotonnes, leaving a substantial gap if production capacity does not increase.

Demand for lithium batteries for energy-storage capacity for renewable electricity will put further pressure on lithium production, says Zhikao Li, a chemical and biological engineer at Monash University.

About 25% of this lithium is projected to come from parts of Chile and Argentina. Here, producers pump naturally occurring lithium-rich brine from underground aquifers into large evaporation ponds. Over a period of months or years, sunlight and wind concentrate the brine until lithium-rich salts can be recovered. The process is effective, but inefficient, say scientists. Brine contains many dissolved salts, each with distinct solubilities. As the water evaporates, the least soluble salts crystallize first, whereas lithium salts are some of the last to separate. Up to 50% of the lithium can be left behind in evaporation ponds, and extra fresh water is often needed to purify the remaining metal.

“The key limitation for existing processes is the fresh water, and also it’s a very slow process,” says Huanting Wang, who is working on alternative extraction methods at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia.

The water use is particularly concerning because brine deposits tend to exist in arid or semi-arid regions where fresh water is already scarce, says Ehsan Vahidi, a who studies metallurgical engineering at the University of Nevada in Reno.

Brine mining has impacts for local Indigenous communities and damages wetland ecosystems, say researchers.

Greener alternatives

Direct lithium extraction is an alternative method that research teams and companies are exploring. These systems use membranes, solvents and electrochemical processes to selectively remove lithium ions from brine.

One possible strategy is being developed by Wang's team at Monash University. The team began by evaporating the brine so that it formed a solid salt mixture and then used acetone and ethanol to selectively dissolve lithium salts while leaving most other compounds behind. In a laboratory study published last month, they report that the process recovered around 95% of the lithium present1.

The method substantially reduces freshwater use compared to traditional methods, the researchers say. And the method could be coupled with solar-powered systems that capture and condense the evaporated water, allowing it to be recycled instead of being lost to the atmosphere. The solvents could also be recovered and reused.

Wang says that the technique could eventually be used to recover lithium present in industrial waste streams and mining residues, which are otherwise wasted.

Peter Sherrell, a materials scientist at RMIT University, Melbourne, says this approach has several advantages over existing methods, such as the high rate of lithium recovery and the fact that the solvents can be recovered and reused. But whether the industry will invest in the technology so it can be used in the real world remains to be seen, he adds.

rss_12_1785526798.title: Fires in Europe are breaking records: here’s what the future holds
rss_12_1785526798.text:
Firefighters watch a blaze west of Madrid. Credit: UME-OCP/Cover Images/Reuters

Fuelled by an unprecedented heatwave, the powerful fires scorching France and Spain are breaking records or are on the verge of doing so — and there are still months to go in the fire season.

“We have been telling society this is going to happen, that we are going to have larger, more catastrophic, more dangerous fires,” says Cristina Santín, who studies wildfires and is at the University of Oviedo in Mieres, Spain. “And now they are here.”

Satellite data show that 91,000 hectares have burnt in France as of 29 July (see ‘Europe ablaze’), smashing the previous record of just over 66,000 hectares burnt during the entire fire season, which generally lasts from March until the end of October. In Spain, more than 200,000 hectares have burnt — well above average this early in the season — and a fire close to Madrid has become the largest single fire in the country’s history.

Source: European Forest Fire Information System

The fires have led to the evacuation of hundreds of thousands of people. Ministers from Spain and the United Kingdom issued a joint statement on 29 July saying that “this summer’s wildfires demonstrated that climate change was now a national security emergency facing Europe and threatening our way of life”.

Scientists say the blazes could mark a shift in southern Europe’s fire patterns: after decades of relative quiet, the region’s fire regime is starting to resemble that of notoriously combustible places such as California. A study1 published today in Scientific Reports shows that the intensity of hot, dry fire-promoting weather in parts of France and Spain was up to 50% higher in the past decade than in the period between 1981 and 2010. Parts of Spain and Portugal that once saw fewer than ten days of highly fire-promoting conditions in a year now see up to 25.

The intense fires seen in Europe this year and the previous few years suggest that heightened fire risk seems to be becoming a reality, researchers say. The fire burning near Madrid nearly destroyed a NASA complex used to communicate with deep-space spacecraft. Firefighters in France battled a towering ‘fire cloud’ intense enough to generate its own erratic weather — the first ever observed in the nation. And another heatwave is developing.

Quiet before the firestorm

To understand trends in fire risk in southern Europe, Raúl Cordero, a meteorologist at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, and his colleagues compiled records as far back as the 1980s on the area of burnt land and the number of fires in Portugal, Spain, France, Italy and Greece1.

The researchers found that between 2016 and 2025, wildfire activity across this region was substantially lower than between 1981 and 2010. There were fewer fires, and, apart from in Portugal, which saw huge fires in 2017, less area burnt. The number of fires declined by at least 40% in each country.

That decline is all the more remarkable given that fire weather — the hot, dry, windy conditions that make it easier for vegetation to burn — has seen the opposite pattern. “Europe used to be kind of an anomaly,” says Cordero. In the past few years, it was having higher temperatures than before and a higher fire risk “but the burned area was going down”.

You’re not imagining it: extreme wildfires are now more common

Rising temperatures driven by anthropogenic climate change are the main factor behind the increase in fire weather, says Cordero. “When you have a heatwave, you are also going to have extreme fire-weather conditions.”

This year, the multiple heatwaves that have baked Europe since May have parched vegetation, priming it to burn. This pattern is similar to the combination of intense heat and subsequent record-breaking fires that burnt in Spain in 2025, says Cordero. And this pattern is set to repeat. Previous research2 projected that the increasing temperatures this century will substantially boost fire risk in Europe. “This is the kind of trend that is unstoppable,” says Santín.

rss_13_1785526800.title: How I use statistics and my law degree to fight human-rights abuses
rss_13_1785526800.text:
Mary Gray has applied statistical and legal arguments to make recommendations for how governments and organizations can address genocide and other human-rights atrocities, as well as workplace discrimination. Now in her 80s, her career as a lawyer, statistician and mathematician at the American University in Washington DC continues. “In spite of the fact that I have a lot of white hair, I’m not retired yet,” she says.

Some researchers focus on a handful of narrowly defined problems. But Gray’s work is vast in comparison.

She has trained investigators for the International Criminal Court in the Hague, the Netherlands, to determine the extent of human-rights violations and genocide. Closer to home, she has worked to combat sex-, race- and age-based discrimination and to create opportunities in US academia for people from diverse backgrounds.

As founding president of the Association for Women in Mathematics from 1971 to 74, Gray established networks and support for female colleagues and advocated for a more equitable and inclusive culture across the discipline. In 2022, when the association established its Mary and Alfie Gray Award for Social Justice — which is named after Gray and her mathematician husband, who died in 1998 — the organization described Mary Gray as having “lived her life in the pursuit of mathematics excellence and social justice”. Alongside her academic research and teaching, Gray has volunteered with both Amnesty International and Statistics Without Borders, an organization that provides pro bono statistics and data-science services to improve human welfare worldwide.

Why I made a river my co-author

Several years after publishing her PhD thesis on abstract mathematics (titled Radical Subcategories) in 1967, she had a realization. “I was never going to, I would say win a Nobel prize, except there are no Nobel Prizes in mathematics,” she says. Instead, she found a natural fit when asked by colleagues to work on some statistical problems about whether there was sex or race discrimination in the selection of White House fellows — young professionals undertaking work-experience placements at the highest levels of the US federal government. So she bolstered her background in statistics and decided to focus on “more practical applications”, she says.

Many researchers would be satisfied with dual expertise in mathematics and statistics. But it was one issue — inequitable retirement benefits for men and women — that fuelled Gray’s decision to earn a law degree.

Becoming a lawyer

In the 1970s, while Gray was examining the retirement benefits she was offered through the Teachers Insurance and Annuity Association (TIAA), which handles retirement benefits for many professors in the United States, she noticed sex discrimination. “When you got an annuity from the TIAA, there was a difference in what was paid out for men or women,” she recalls. If a man and a woman had the same accumulated amount of retirement funds and were retiring at the same age, the monthly payments that the man would receive would be 15% more than the woman’s. And, Gray says, the argument from the insurance company was that women will live longer, so they will eventually get more payouts and everything will be equal.

When Gray didn’t accept that reasoning, the insurance company stated that she didn’t understand the law. Her retort was to go to the Washington College of Law at the American University, where she graduated in 1979 as one of the top students and then joined the Maryland State Bar Association.

Eventually, Gray helped to end those discriminatory policies in retirement benefit packages. She and an economist colleague, Barbara Bergman, contributed their published research and expert testimony to a 1983 US Supreme Court case. In Arizona Governing Committee v. Norris, the country’s highest court ruled that discrepancies in retirement plan benefits for men and women were illegal on the basis of sex discrimination.

Gray and her colleague’s basic argument before the court was statistical. “If you look at the normal distribution of when people die, you would find that there are two normal curves: one for men and one for women,” Gray says. Those curves have about 86% overlap, meaning that a large number of people are likely to die inside the same age range regardless of their sex, she notes. In other words, women aren’t guaranteed to outlive their male colleagues.

Looking back, Gray is glad that she chose to study mathematics before later pursuing legal training. “I’m glad that I did it all, but I think for me, it was more productive than it would have been the other way around,” she says. It would be helpful if more mathematicians and statisticians cross-trained in legal scholarship and vice versa, she notes. When human rights or lives are at stake, having both numbers and the law on your side can help to strengthen arguments, she says.

Mary Gray was inspired to pursue a law degree after uncovering sex-discrimination in US academics’ retirement benefits policies.

Perseverance meets problems

Char Mollison, a specialist in the management of non-profit organizations at the Center on Nonprofits, Philanthropy, and Social Enterprise at George Mason University in Fairfax, Virginia, describes Gray as “mission-driven” and “not driven by self-aggrandizement”.

The two met in around 1980 through a women’s rights organization called the Women’s Equity Action League (WEAL). Mollison was serving as WEAL’s executive director, and Gray was the elected chair of its board. Gray had a reputation for “getting women into mathematics” and “she was often an expert witness in class-action lawsuits promoting equity for women”, Mollison says. She was impressed with Gray’s ability to encourage collaboration and respectful dialogue while keeping the group from getting stuck in endless debates about divisive public policy and legislative advocacy issues.

“In an advocacy organization like WEAL, you have all kinds of points of view about what to do next,” Mollison says. Board meetings could become heated as the group discussed what compromises it might need to make to bring about desired policy or legal changes. Mollison says that Gray was known as a fair and empathetic listener, but she also kept the meetings — and votes — moving. “She knew that as an organization, we had to make a decision and move forward.”
